title: Authority Gets Compliance, Trust Gets Commitment
author: Kurt Mueller
source: kurtmueller.substack.com (Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership), October 16, 2026
summary: Kurt Mueller argues that positional authority buys a leader compliance but not the commitment that comes from being trusted. He starts from Charles Feltman's definition of trust as choosing to risk making something of value vulnerable to another person's actions, and says that definition works for both building and repairing trust. He lists what a trusted leader gains, including earlier warning about problems, openness to hard feedback, willingness to take risks, and followership when the right answer is unclear. A quick trust test asks whether words and actions match, since people believe the behavior over the statement. He gives a practical scenario in which a leader invites an opposing perspective on a work-allocation change, listens without defending, and summarizes before responding. For damaged trust he says to start with understanding why it was damaged rather than defending intentions, then replace the offending behavior with a visible, repeatable action.
points: Compliance can be ordered, but the extra influence leaders want (early problem reporting, risk taking, followership under uncertainty) only comes from earned trust.
Words that contradict behavior teach the opposite lesson, so a leader who says "bring me problems early" and then criticizes the messenger has taught the team to hide problems.
Inviting an opposing perspective, listening without defending, and summarizing what you heard shows respect even when the decision does not change.
Rebuilding trust begins with showing you understand why it was damaged; explanation before understanding sounds like justification.
Trust becomes developmental when reflection turns into behavior, so ask a colleague what you do that builds or weakens confidence and pick one action for this week.
quotes: You may have the authority to direct your team’s actions, but that doesn’t mean you have earned their trust.
Trust is built slowly—but can be damaged surprisingly quickly. You can spend months establishing leadership credibility and weaken it with one poorly handled situation.
Your words said one thing. Your behavior taught something completely different. People usually trust the behavior. Not the statement.
Listen without interrupting or defending your decision. Then summarize what you heard before responding.
You may eventually need to explain your reasoning. But explanation before understanding can sound like justification.
The first step in rebuilding trust is often demonstrating that you understand why it was damaged.
Instead, identify the behavior that created the problem and replace it with a visible, repeatable action.
